newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE TAKES POLE IN ARGENTINA.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE TAKES POLE IN ARGENTINA.

text.p: World championship favourite Jacques Villeneuve continued his dominance of this year's Formula One series when he grabbed pole position on Saturday for Sunday's Argentine Grand Prix.

The 26-year-old Canadian, driving a Williams-Renault, clocked a fastest time of one minute and 24.473 seconds on the bumpy track to shatter the old qualifying record for the track by more than six seconds.
It was a stunning performance by Villeneuve, who had been suffering from a stomach disorder. It also said much for the massive technical advances of the cars since a 'tyre war' began this year.
Villeneuve's Williams team mate Heinz-Harald Frentzen wound up second-quickest to claim a place alongside the Canadian on the front row of the grid for Sunday's 72-lap race.

It was Villeneuve's third pole position of the season, his fourth in succession and the sixth of his career. He shares the lead in the world drivers' championship with Briton David Coulthard with 10 points after two of the 17 races on the calendar.

Frenchman Olivier Panis in a Prost, using the new Bridgestone tyres as opposed to the Goodyears of the Williams team, claimed third place ahead of double world champion Michael Schumacher of Germany in a Goodyear-shod Ferrari.

Brazilian Rubens Barrichello, in a Jordan with Bridgestone tyres, was fifth and Ralf Schumacher, 21-year-old younger brother of Michael, was sixth for Jordan, using Goodyears, as they qualified for their 100th Grand Prix.
The race will be the 600th Formula One world championship event since the series was inaugurated in 1950.

Villeneuve's pole was also the 100th for the Williams team on a day when Panis achieved his best-ever qualifying position and Barrichello claimed the Stewart team's first top 10 starting place on the grid.

Britain's Damon Hill, the 1996 world champion, qualified 13th for Arrows, the team whose future was the centre of speculation at the circuit after reports that they are to have a new car, designed by Briton John Barnard and powered by Honda engines, next year.
Villeneuve was happy to claim pole but said he was still struggling with his illness. "I hoped it would be better today," he said. "But it isn't."
He warned that the first corner of the race would be a tight affair on the bumpy circuit but said his car felt strong and good and that he was confident.

Villeneuve said the extra performance in the cars came mostly from the vastly improved tyres this year. "Last year, they were too hard on this circuit and this year they are much better, much softer."
Frentzen said he had found a much-improved set up which had improved his performance from Brazil, where he languished badly and came home ninth.
